summary: Defines OSPF-xTE, an experimental traffic engineering extension to OSPF that uses new TE link state advertisements to spread TE metrics and builds a separate TE database. Nodes that do not support it are unaffected. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: An experiment that adds a second, special map for planning traffic routes, without confusing routers that only read the normal map.

questions: how does ospf-xte differ from rfc3630
subtitle: Experimental traffic engineering extensions to OSPF for managing network resources

tldr.problem: The OSPF routing protocol was designed for shortest-path routing and does not carry information about network links' capacity, reliability, or other attributes needed for traffic engineering—reserving paths for specific traffic flows.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF-xTE adds new link state advertisements (LSAs) that carry traffic engineering metrics like available bandwidth and link reliability. It maintains a separate TE-specific database so non-TE routers are unaffected, and nodes can compute constraint-based paths for engineering traffic.
tldr.outcome: This experimental approach was superseded by RFC 3630 (Opaque LSA extensions), which the OSPF working group preferred for its compatibility and proven approach. However, OSPF-xTE introduced ideas about mixing TE and non-TE routers and supporting non-packet networks.

today: RFC 4973 is an Experimental RFC that has not been obsoleted, but RFC 3630 is the consensus OSPF TE extension in widespread use. OSPF-xTE remains available for research and experimental deployments.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering and OSPF
sections.content:
Traffic Engineering is the practice of directing network traffic along specific paths to better use network resources. Instead of every packet taking the shortest path (which can overload some links), traffic engineering reserves paths with known available capacity for specific traffic flows.

The standard OSPF routing protocol has no way to advertise which links have extra capacity or other characteristics needed for traffic engineering. OSPF-xTE solves this by adding new link state advertisements that carry traffic engineering metrics. The key insight is that an autonomous system (AS) may contain both traffic-engineered routers and regular routers. OSPF-xTE ensures that regular routers are not disrupted by the extra TE information.
sections.eli5: Regular routers follow the shortest path, like cars taking the fastest route to work. Traffic engineering is like a traffic manager saying "hey, this highway is congested, use this other route instead." OSPF-xTE teaches routers to understand these instructions without breaking existing routes.

sections.title: Design: Separate TE and Native Databases
sections.content:
OSPF-xTE creates two separate link-state databases within each router. The native LSDB contains traditional OSPF topology information for standard IP routing. The TE-LSDB contains only TE link state advertisements and represents the TE network topology.

This separation has important consequences: non-TE routers in the network never see or process the TE advertisements, so they are completely unaffected. TE routers can compute constraint-based shortest paths (CSPF) by consulting the TE-LSDB. OSPF-xTE nodes use locally-scoped Opaque LSAs (type 9) to discover other TE-capable neighbors and build the TE topology, separate from standard OSPF adjacency.

In networks where some routers are TE-capable and others are not, the designated router exchanges different sets of LSAs: TE LSAs only with TE neighbors, and native LSAs with all neighbors.
sections.eli5: Each TE-aware router keeps two maps. One map shows the regular network (like normal). The other map shows which links are reserved for special traffic. Non-TE routers only see the first map, so they do not get confused.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering Metrics and LSA Types
sections.content:
OSPF-xTE defines new TE LSA types to carry traffic engineering information. The TE-Router LSA (type 0x81) advertises the TE capabilities of a router, such as support for traffic prioritization or bandwidth provisioning. Each router-TE LSA contains TLVs (Tag-Length-Value structures) describing the router's TE functions.

The TE-Link LSA (type 0x81) contains link-TE TLVs that describe a link's TE metrics: available bandwidth, link reliability, color (for traffic policy), and membership in shared risk link groups (SRLGs). A TE-Incremental-Link-Update LSA (type 0x8d) allows advertising only the TE metrics that changed, reducing flooding overhead when dynamic metrics like available bandwidth fluctuate.

Additional LSA types support TE across multiple areas and non-packet networks such as SONET/TDM and optical networks, making OSPF-xTE applicable beyond packet switching.
sections.eli5: OSPF-xTE says "this router can do traffic engineering" and "this link has 50 Mbps available" using special messages. It only sends an update when a number changes, so it does not spam the network with constant updates.

sections.title: Operation in Mixed and Peer Networks
sections.content:
OSPF-xTE is designed to operate in networks that mix TE-capable and non-TE routers. This requires careful handling: a TE router can have both TE links (used for traffic engineering) and native links (used for regular IP traffic). In a mixed network, some routers are TE-capable (running OSPF-xTE) and others are not.

A key design goal is to allow TE links to be physically isolated from native links, or to share physical links while assigning capacity separately to each. For example, an operator could assign 30% of a link's bandwidth to TE and 70% to best-effort IP. This prevents TE traffic from being disrupted by ordinary routing and keeps the networks independently manageable.

In a peer network, OSPF-xTE supports both packet networks (MPLS) and non-packet networks (SONET/TDM, optical) in the same AS, with external proxy routers capable of advertising on behalf of non-OSPF nodes.
sections.eli5: Some routers understand traffic engineering and some do not. You can draw special lines in the network just for engineered traffic, or you can split a regular link between regular traffic and special traffic.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Alternatives
sections.content:
OSPF-xTE was published as an Experimental RFC. At the time of publication, the OSPF working group noted that RFC 3630 (Opaque LSA-based TE extensions) was the consensus approach and was already considered sufficient for known traffic engineering requirements. RFC 3630 was preferred because it was already in use and the cost of migrating to OSPF-xTE exceeded its benefits.

OSPF-xTE remains available for experimental use and introduces valuable concepts: cleanly separating TE and non-TE topologies, efficiently handling rapid metric changes, and extending traffic engineering to non-packet networks. However, the industry converged on the RFC 3630 approach for MPLS TE in OSPF networks.
sections.eli5: This experiment was interesting but the industry chose a different way (RFC 3630) that was already working. OSPF-xTE's ideas are still useful, but it is not deployed.
